big: Rohan wants to buy a share, but he has a bank account and nothing else. Between his bank and the exchange, he needs two more accounts, and he needs to know which order to place.

lines: Why do I need a demat account and a trading account? Is one not enough?
The demat account holds your shares, like a bank holds your money. The trading account is the doorway for placing the order. They work together with your bank.

rows: He places an order in the trading account
Money leaves his linked bank account
The shares are credited to his demat account
Kept by depositories NSDL and CDSL
note: A demat account holds shares in electronic form, so there is no paper certificate to lose.

title: Accounts and orders
stops: A demat account holds shares digitally
A limit order always gets filled
A trading account is where you place orders
A stop-loss order guarantees the exit price
caps: Shares are kept in electronic form, with records held by NSDL and CDSL.
A limit order fills only at your price or better, so it may not fill.
The trading account connects your bank and demat account.
In a fast fall, a stop-loss may fill below the level you set.

alt: Bars comparing how likely a market order and a limit order are to execute and how much price control each gives
caps: A market order buys at the best price available right now.
It almost always executes, but you do not control the price.
A limit order buys only at your chosen price or better.
You control the price, but it may never fill. These numbers only illustrate the idea.

q: Meena wants to buy a share only if it falls to ₹500 or lower. Which order should she use?
opts: No order, and wait to be called
why: A market order buys at once at the current price, which may be higher.
A stop-loss is meant to sell a holding when the price falls, not to buy.
A limit order buys only at her price or better, so it waits for ₹500.
Nobody calls her. She needs to place an order for any trade to happen.

q: Rohan bought at ₹200 and set a stop-loss at ₹180. The price gaps down to ₹170 overnight. What may happen?
opts: The sale is certain at exactly ₹180
The shares are returned to the company
The order cancels itself and he gains
why: In a fast fall, a stop-loss can fill below the level that was set.
A stop-loss does not guarantee the price, so exactly ₹180 is not certain.
Shares are not returned to a company when a stop-loss is triggered.
A cancelled order would not create a gain, as the price fell.

q: What does a demat account do?
opts: Places the buy and sell orders
Pays the interest on a loan
Issues new shares to the public
why: Orders are placed through the trading account, not the demat account.
A demat account works like a bank for shares, kept electronically.
A demat account has no connection with paying interest on a loan.
New shares are issued by the company, and not by a demat account.

q: Who keeps the records of shares held in demat form?
opts: The shop where Meena bought her phone
why: A police station does not keep share records for investors.
A phone shop has no link to holdings of shares.
A newspaper office does not hold investor records.
NSDL and CDSL are the two depositories that hold these records.

pts: A demat account holds shares. A trading account places orders.
A limit order fills only at your price or better, so it may not fill.
A stop-loss may fill below your level in a fast fall.
